correctness.rationale: The morphism satisfies W_k=W_{k-1}W_{k-2}W_{k-2} and an alternating final-letter recurrence. The source proves by parity-aligned desubstitution that W_{k-2} occurs in W_k only at positions 0, 2^{k-1} and 3·2^{k-2}, for all k>=3. This supports absence and both proper-factor occurrences for the two boundary obstructions. The global forbidden families arise by iterating Psi(v)=mu(v) with first symbol removed, starting from 0000 and 1001; a hereditary inverse-morphism/parity argument proves absence while separate induction tracks positions of the truncated prefix/suffix occurrences at each level. Two initial-letter towers, distinct lengths, and the k=3 exceptional collision check establish pairwise distinct 2k-1 witnesses. Independently constructed W_k and tested the three-position lemma and all specified witness absences/prefix/suffix inclusions for k=3..10, giving 5,7,9,11,13,15,17,19 witnesses. These tests do not prove the all-k lower bound; the substitution induction is the proof. No general upper bound or full antidictionary enumeration is asserted.

originality.rationale: Currie (2023) classifies good words avoiding the infinite period-doubling factor-language patterns by a desubstitution theorem. That covers global prohibited patterns but not the two finite-prefix boundary obstructions or the quantitative at-least-2k-1 count. Pinho et al. 2009 and Barton et al. 2014 define and compute minimal absent factors for arbitrary strings, not an all-level symbolic list for the period-doubling dyadic prefixes. Nearest published result on period-doubling prefix attractors evaluates a different statistic. Best-of-knowledge original constructive bound; equivalent finite-prefix formulas in unindexed automatic-word literature remain a risk.
residual_risks: A specialised but unindexed automatic-word/minimal-absent-factor study might contain the identical log lower bound.
The theorem proves at least 2k-1, not equality; finite exact checks k3–8 must not be extrapolated.

value.rationale: Minimal absent factors are the finite word’s antidictionary and are a standard measure of negative substring information. Showing at least logarithmically many explicit and structurally different obstructions in highly ordered dyadic prefixes, separated into hereditary global and endpoint-generated families, is a motivated all-scale structural result. It is not a claim of complete census and not merely a finite computation.

final_claim: Let mu(0)=01 and mu(1)=00, W_k=mu^k(0) of length 2^k, k>=3. The finite binary word W_k has at least 2k-1 pairwise distinct minimal absent contiguous factors, explicitly 11; for every j=0,...,k-3 the two words Psi^j(0000) and Psi^j(1001) with Psi(v)=mu(v) after deleting its initial symbol; and two finite-boundary words c_{k-2} W_{k-2}0 and c_{k-1} W_{k-1}, where c_j is the last symbol of W_j. Every witness is absent while both immediate proper prefix and suffix occur. This is an all-k constructive lower bound only; equality for all k is not asserted.
limitations: Only a constructive lower bound for binary dyadic period-doubling prefixes k>=3, not an all-k total antidictionary classification.
Does not extend automatically to arbitrary lengths or other constant-length morphisms.
